text.en: In 1960, 17 African countries gained independence — more than in any other single year in history.
In 1989, the year Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web, the golden toad was seen for the last time in Costa Rica's forests.
Star Wars came out in May 1977, and in September France carried out its last execution by guillotine. The death penalty was abolished there only in 1981.
1957: the USSR launched the first satellite, and six countries signed the Treaty of Rome, the seed of the future EU.
Gagarin flew into space in April 1961; that August, the Berlin Wall went up.
Tetris was invented in Moscow in 1984, five years before Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web at CERN.
1957: Ghana became one of the first countries in sub-Saharan Africa to throw off colonial rule, and the USSR launched the first satellite.
Spring 1953: the structure of DNA was published on 25 April, and on 29 May Hillary and Tenzing reached the top of Everest.
In autumn 1956 the world watched two crises at once: the Anglo-French landing at the Suez Canal and Soviet tanks in Budapest.

The architect of the Sydney Opera House never saw it finished. Jørn Utzon quit in 1966, vowing never to return to Australia, and kept his word: he died in 2008 without ever seeing the completed building.

Einstein was offered the presidency of Israel. In November 1952, after Chaim Weizmann died, Prime Minister Ben-Gurion offered him the ceremonial post; Einstein replied that he was deeply moved but could not accept.
The aircraft 'black box' was dreamed up by an Australian. In 1953 Melbourne scientist David Warren proposed a device that would record not just instrument readings but also the voices in the cockpit.
The structure of DNA was first announced in a pub. On 28 February 1953 Francis Crick interrupted lunch at The Eagle in Cambridge to declare that he and Watson had discovered 'the secret of life'.
News that Everest had been climbed reached London just in time for the coronation, on the morning of 2 June 1953, as Elizabeth II was crowned.
Einstein's brain weighed 1,230 grams, well within the normal human range. After the 1955 autopsy, pathologist Thomas Harvey preserved it for science and cut it into 170 pieces.

The Guinness Book of Records was created to settle pub arguments. The idea came from Sir Hugh Beaver, managing director of the Guinness brewery; twins Norris and Ross McWhirter compiled it in 1955, and it was a bestseller by Christmas.
The 1956 Melbourne Olympics were partly held in Stockholm. Australia's strict animal quarantine meant the equestrian events were staged in Sweden, five months before the rest of the Games.
The first Eurovision, in 1956, had just seven countries, each singing two songs. The host, Switzerland, won, and juries were still allowed to vote for their own entries.

Both Play-Doh and bubble wrap began as wallpaper products. Play-Doh was a 1930s cleaner for sooty wallpaper before becoming a toy in the 1950s, and bubble wrap was a failed 1957 attempt at textured wallpaper.

The Frisbee is named after a bakery and started out as the 'Pluto Platter'. Yale students tossed empty pie tins from the Frisbie Pie Company, so in 1957 the maker renamed its plastic disc the Frisbee.

Until 2012, only two people had been to the bottom of the Mariana Trench, six times fewer than had walked on the Moon. Piccard and Walsh dived in 1960; twelve astronauts walked on the Moon in 1969–1972.

Decca Records turned the Beatles down. They auditioned on 1 January 1962, but the label signed Brian Poole and the Tremeloes instead. A year later the Beatles recorded their first album in a single day, elsewhere.

The 1964 Tokyo Olympics were the first broadcast overseas without flying tapes across. Earlier Games went by plane; this time the signal reached the US via Syncom 3, the first geostationary communications satellite.
The Jules Rimet Trophy was stolen twice. In 1966 Pickles the dog found it; after Brazil won it outright in 1970, it was stolen again in 1983 and has never been recovered.
Sweden switched to driving on the right despite a referendum. In 1955, 83% voted to stay on the left, but car numbers kept rising, and in 1967 the country changed sides anyway, in a single morning.

Humanity's most famous ancestor is named after a Beatles song. In 1974 the expedition camp in Ethiopia played 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds' loudly all evening, so the newly found skeleton became Lucy.

Almost every high jumper today goes over the bar backwards, thanks to one American. Dick Fosbury won gold at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics with his odd back-first leap, and the 'Fosbury flop' soon became the norm.
The computer that guided Apollo to the Moon had about 4 kilobytes of working memory: 2,048 sixteen-bit words of magnetic core. Its programs sat in a separate read-only memory of 36,864 words.

The first session on ARPANET, the internet's ancestor, crashed after two letters. On 29 October 1969, three months after the Moon landing, student Charley Kline began typing 'login' and the Stanford computer went down.
In 1971 astronaut Alan Shepard played golf on the Moon. He fixed a club head to a sampling-tool handle and swung one-handed at two balls; the second, he said, went 'miles and miles and miles'.

The first microprocessor was ordered for a Japanese calculator. In 1969 Busicom asked Intel to design a set of chips, and engineer Marcian Hoff proposed putting the processor on a single chip: the Intel 4004.

The US–China thaw began when an American table-tennis player missed his bus. At the 1971 World Championships in Nagoya, Glenn Cowan hopped on the Chinese team's bus, where world champion Zhuang Zedong struck up a conversation.
The first call from a handheld mobile phone went to a rival. On 3 April 1973 Motorola engineer Martin Cooper rang his counterpart at competitor Bell Labs from a Manhattan sidewalk.

In one month of 1974 a soldier who had ignored the end of the war for 29 years gave up, and an army that had waited 2,200 years was found: Onoda surrendered on 10 March, the Terracotta Army turned up on 29 March.

Hiroo Onoda was not the last soldier of World War II. Private Teruo Nakamura held out even longer and was arrested in Indonesia on 18 December 1974. Japan's government had declared Onoda dead back in 1959.

In 1975 an American became a millionaire selling ordinary stones. Ad man Gary Dahl packed pebbles in boxes with air holes, like a pet carrier, and in about six months sold nearly 1.5 million Pet Rocks at almost $4 each.
'Johnny B. Goode' is now travelling through interstellar space: on 25 August 2012 Voyager 1, carrying its Golden Record, became the first human-made craft to enter interstellar space.
The last person to catch smallpox naturally was a hospital cook in Somalia. Ali Maow Maalin recovered in 1977 and later worked on the polio vaccination campaign in Somalia himself.
Pac-Man, his creator said, was dreamed up at lunch while looking at a pizza with a slice missing. Toru Iwatani later added that he also rounded off the Japanese character for 'mouth', 口.

To prove that bacteria cause gastritis, an Australian doctor infected himself. In 1984 Barry Marshall swallowed a culture of Helicobacter pylori and fell ill; in 2005 he and Robin Warren won the Nobel Prize.

Hubble's mirror was ground wrong by 2.2 micrometres, dozens of times thinner than a hair. That was enough to blur its view: in 1993 astronauts flew up to fit corrective optics, in effect a pair of glasses.
The world's first webcam watched a coffee pot. In 1991 Cambridge University computer scientists pointed a camera at their coffee machine so colleagues would not make a wasted trip to an empty pot.
A single eruption cooled the whole planet. After the Philippines' Mount Pinatubo blew in 1991, a sulphuric haze spread around the Earth and global temperatures fell by about 0.5 °C in 1991–1993.
The first text message ever sent was a Christmas greeting. On 3 December 1992 engineer Neil Papworth sent two words from a computer to a colleague's phone: 'Merry Christmas'.

Nollywood began with a videotape trader. The writer of Living in Bondage had no money, so he teamed up with Kenneth Nnebue, a businessman importing VHS tapes from Taiwan. They shot on a camcorder and sold it straight to video.
Edmund Hillary appeared on a banknote while still alive. His portrait has been on New Zealand's $5 note since 1992, and he insisted the backdrop be Aoraki / Mount Cook rather than Everest.
Dolly the sheep was named after Dolly Parton. She was cloned from a mammary gland cell, and Ian Wilmut joked that they couldn't think of a more impressive pair of glands than Parton's.
One of Deep Blue's moves in the 1997 match may have been a glitch. In game one, the story goes, it could not pick a move and fell back on a fail-safe. Kasparov won that game but lost the match.

In 1999 NASA lost a Mars probe over pounds and newtons. A contractor's software gave thruster impulse in pound-force seconds while NASA expected newton-seconds: an error of 4.45 times that sent the craft too close to the planet.
Bhutan is thought to be the last country in the world to get television, which arrived only in 1999. Before that, owning a TV set had been banned there by a 1989 ruling.

Australia's first Winter Olympic gold went to the man in last place. In the 2002 short-track 1,000 m final Steven Bradbury trailed far behind, until the whole field ahead of him crashed on the final corner.
The first YouTube video is 19 seconds long and filmed by an elephant enclosure. On 23 April 2005 co-founder Jawed Karim stood at San Diego Zoo and remarked on how long the elephants' trunks were.

In the Burj Khalifa the sun sets at different times on different floors. Residents above the 80th floor break the Ramadan fast two minutes later than at ground level, and above the 150th, three minutes later.

The deep-learning revolution ran on two gaming graphics cards. AlexNet did not fit in the memory of a single Nvidia GTX 580, so it was split across two, and in 2012 it won the ImageNet contest by a wide margin.

One poet wrote the anthems of two countries. Rabindranath Tagore wrote and composed both India's 'Jana Gana Mana' and Bangladesh's 'Amar Sonar Bangla', and Sri Lanka's anthem was inspired by his work.
George Lucas secured the merchandising and sequel rights to Star Wars before filming, after the 1973 hit American Graffiti. At first only one company, Kenner, agreed to make toys from the film.
The name of the man behind Sputnik and Gagarin's spacecraft was a state secret. Sergei Korolev was known only as the 'Chief Designer'; the public learned who he was from his obituary in January 1966.
The first Sputnik beeped for only three weeks, until its batteries died, then circled the Earth silently for over two more months. It burned up on 4 January 1958 after 1,440 orbits.

The Soviets recruited space dogs from the streets, reasoning that Moscow strays were already used to cold and hunger. Laika, the first animal in orbit, was originally called Kudryavka, 'Little Curly'.
Humanity first saw the far side of the Moon in 1959. The Soviet probe Luna 3 took 29 pictures in 40 minutes, developed the film on board and transmitted the images to Earth.

No camera caught Khrushchev banging his shoe at the UN. On 12 October 1960 a photo shows a shoe on his desk, but whether he pounded it is still debated; biographer William Taubman, after interviewing witnesses, concluded he did.
A space dog's daughter lived in the White House. Khrushchev gave the Kennedys Pushinka, a puppy of Strelka; she had a litter with the Kennedys' dog, and the president jokingly called them 'pupniks'.
Gagarin landed separately from his capsule, by parachute, after ejecting at 7 km. FAI rules then required a pilot to land inside his craft for a record, and the USSR admitted the truth only in 1971.

Valentina Tereshkova is the only woman ever to fly in space alone. Before becoming a cosmonaut she worked in a textile mill and secretly took up parachuting; her call sign in orbit was 'Chaika', Seagull.

The Moscow–Washington hotline was once cut by a Finnish farmer's plough and another time by a Danish bulldozer. And a Soviet diplomat asked the US Secretary of State what the first message, about a 'quick brown fox', meant.

The first man to walk in space was, ten years later, the first to shake an American's hand in orbit. Alexei Leonov stepped out of Voskhod 2 in 1965 and in 1975 greeted Thomas Stafford through the Soyuz hatch.

One of the first computer-versus-computer chess matches was won by a program from Moscow. In 1966–67 a program from the ITEP institute played Stanford's Kotok-McCarthy program by telegraph for nine months, and won.

The first spacecraft to make a soft landing on another planet was Soviet. On 15 December 1970 Venera 7 touched down on Venus and transmitted from the surface for about 20 minutes: it was 475 °C there.

In 1989 PepsiCo bartered for 17 Soviet submarines. The USSR paid for Pepsi syrup with Stolichnaya vodka, and when vodka sales fell, with decommissioned vessels — submarines, a cruiser, a frigate and a destroyer — for PepsiCo to resell.

Sergei Krikalev left Earth from the USSR and came back to Russia. He was aboard Mir when the Soviet Union dissolved, staying 311 days, twice as long as planned — earning the nickname 'the last Soviet citizen'.

The record for the longest single spaceflight, 437 days, belongs to the physician Valeri Polyakov. He spent over 14 months on Mir to test whether humans could survive a trip to Mars, and on landing said: 'We can fly to Mars.'
In February 2012 Russian scientists drilled through 3,768 metres of ice to reach Lake Vostok beneath Antarctica. Its water is thought to have been sealed off from the surface for millions of years.

The first people to greet a man back from space were a farm worker and her granddaughter. Near Engels they saw a figure in an orange suit and white helmet come down from the sky and backed away — until Gagarin explained he was one of them.

In 1982 ten-year-old American Samantha Smith wrote to Yuri Andropov asking if he wanted war. Pravda printed her letter; he replied and invited her to the Artek camp, where in 1983 she turned down special lodgings to stay with Soviet children.
Artificial intelligence is older than the Space Age. The term was coined in 1955 for the Dartmouth workshop held in the summer of 1956, while the first satellite flew only in October 1957.
The first woman flew into space when the Beatles had released just one album. Please Please Me came out in March 1963; Valentina Tereshkova launched on 16 June.
Ten days before the Higgs boson was announced, Lonesome George died. The last tortoise of the Pinta Island subspecies died on 24 June 2012; CERN announced its discovery on 4 July.
Brazil's capital is younger than the first satellite. Brasília was inaugurated in April 1960, two and a half years after Sputnik 1, having been built almost from scratch in 41 months.
The Norwegian King’s Guard knighted a penguin. Nils Olav, a king penguin at Edinburgh Zoo and the Guard’s mascot since 1972, became Sir Nils Olav in 2008.

In 1954 'the fastest man on Earth' was a doctor. On a rocket sled John Stapp reached 1,017 km/h and stopped in 1.4 seconds. The 46 g left him briefly blind, but he lived and went on to campaign for car seat belts.

The echo of the Big Bang was first blamed on pigeon droppings. In 1964 Penzias and Wilson could not get rid of noise in their antenna, cleaned out the droppings and evicted the pigeons; the noise was the cosmic background, and won them a Nobel Prize.

The most famous 'alien' signal is named after a margin note. In 1977 astronomer Jerry Ehman circled the sequence '6EQUJ5' on a printout and wrote 'Wow!' beside it. Where those 72 seconds came from is still unknown.

The first pulsar was jokingly named LGM-1, for 'little green men'. In 1967 Cambridge student Jocelyn Bell spotted radio pulses so regular that the team seriously checked whether they could be signals from aliens.

Sticky notes came from a glue that didn't stick well. In 1968 3M chemist Spencer Silver made a weak adhesive nobody had a use for, until colleague Art Fry wanted bookmarks that wouldn't fall out of his church choir hymnal.

The implantable pacemaker came from grabbing the wrong resistor. In 1956 engineer Wilson Greatbatch was building a heart-rhythm recorder, fitted the wrong part, and the circuit began pulsing just like a heartbeat.
Bill Gates says he never claimed '640K ought to be enough for anybody'. The line has been pinned on him since 1981, but he has called it made up, and there is no record of it.
Lemmings do not commit mass suicide. The famous scene was staged in 1958 for Disney's White Wilderness: the animals were brought to Alberta and pushed off a cliff by the crew.
